title: Transfer essay draft
body:
The first dataset I ever cleaned by hand was a spreadsheet of weekly pickups from a local food bank. Half the dates were typed three different ways, and a few rows were plainly duplicates. I spent a weekend fixing them in Python, and when I finally plotted demand by week, the volunteers saw something they had only guessed at: the busiest weeks came right after school breaks. That chart changed how they scheduled shifts. It also changed what I wanted to study.

I came to Diablo Valley College unsure of my direction. My introductory programming course in Python gave me the first real sense that I could build things that mattered to other people. Calculus taught me patience with problems that do not resolve on the first attempt, and I am now working through the second course in the sequence. Along the way I realized that the questions I care about most are not purely technical. They are about how people make decisions with incomplete information, which is why I took microeconomics and statistics as well.

Outside of class, I serve as president of our Data Science Club. Each week we pick a public dataset and work through it together in a Kaggle-style session. Leading the club has taught me that explaining a model clearly is often harder than building it. Some weeks only a few members show up, and I have had to rethink how we choose problems so that beginners and more experienced students both stay engaged.

I also publish small models and demo Spaces on Hugging Face. None of them are large, but each one forced me to think about who would actually use it and what could go wrong when they did. I have learned a lot from these projects, though I am still figuring out how to evaluate them properly.

I want to transfer because I have reached the limits of what I can learn on my own. I need deeper coursework in statistics, computing, and the responsible use of data about real people. I want to learn from faculty whose work connects methods to public problems, and to study alongside classmates who will challenge my assumptions. A university data science program would give me the structure to turn scattered projects into a coherent foundation.

My goal is to use applied machine learning to make public-interest data easier to act on, for food banks, clinics, and local agencies that rarely have an analyst on staff. The food bank dashboard was a small start. I am ready for the training that will let me do that work well, and to bring what I have learned about leading, teaching, and building to the community I join next.
